claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing nano- or microscale phase domains and compositional gradients.
The proposed machine-learning model is trained on experimental mechanical-property data and microstructural descriptors.
The model uses phase fraction, domain size, and compositional mapping as microstructural descriptors.
Hierarchical features such as nano- and microscale domains, phase interfaces, and compositional gradients can be encoded as model inputs.
Correlations between microstructural descriptors and mechanical properties allow the model to capture nonlinear effects.
Correlations between microstructural descriptors and mechanical properties allow the model to capture multiscale effects.
The relevant nonlinear and multiscale effects are difficult for conventional simulations to resolve.
Capturing hierarchical heterogeneity will improve prediction accuracy relative to established physics-based simulations.
The machine-learning model will predict Young's modulus with at least 20% lower mean absolute error than established simulations.
The machine-learning model will predict yield strength with at least 20% lower mean absolute error than established simulations.
The machine-learning model will predict fracture-related behavior with at least 20% lower mean absolute error than established simulations.
The machine-learning model will produce predictions at least 10 times faster than established simulations.
Machine-learning predictions can be produced in seconds, whereas established simulations require hours or days.
Poor characterization of the hierarchical heterostructure may prevent the proposed performance gains.
An insufficient or unrepresentative training dataset may prevent the model from generalizing to new samples.
Overfitting may prevent the model from generalizing to new samples.
The model may fail under extreme loading conditions or for microstructures outside its training domain.
